posts.raw_content:
One of the biggest misconceptions in American politics is that adopting the European welfare state would automatically improve the standard of living of ordinary Americans. Politicians promise free healthcare, free education, generous welfare benefits and government-funded services without adequately addressing the economic consequences of financing such a system. Nothing the government provides is actually free. Every dollar must ultimately come from taxation, borrowing or economic production.

Take Finland, a country frequently praised as an example of what America should become. Finland has experienced virtually no real GDP per capita growth over the past two decades. In fact, its inflation-adjusted GDP per capita in 2025 remained below its 2008 peak. Nearly two decades of technological advancement and economic development have produced remarkably little improvement in economic output per person.

What good is an extensive welfare system if the economy responsible for financing it barely grows? Economic growth is what ultimately allows people to enjoy higher wages, better living standards, greater purchasing power and more opportunities for their children. Redistributing wealth is not the same thing as creating it.

Finland's median annual disposable income, measured in purchasing power terms, is approximately $22,000. Meanwhile, the reported income threshold for the bottom 20% of Americans is approximately $34,500. Although differences in household size and income definitions complicate a direct comparison, these figures challenge the popular assumption that European welfare states necessarily deliver greater material prosperity.

Furthermore, approximately 16.8% of Finland's population is considered at risk of poverty or social exclusion. Despite universal healthcare, publicly funded education, extensive social security programs and relatively high taxation, roughly one in six Finns still falls into this category. The existence of an extensive welfare state clearly does not eliminate economic hardship.

In 2019, Finland's government resigned after failing to implement major healthcare and social welfare reforms intended to address rising costs and the financial pressures of an aging population. Even a wealthy, relatively small and developed country struggled to reconcile its welfare commitments with fiscal reality.

Another factor that rarely receives sufficient attention is Europe's reliance on American military power. For decades, the United States has carried a substantial share of the financial and military burden of Western security.  Finland benefited from the broader security environment underwritten by American power. Had European countries been required to shoulder a substantially greater share of their collective defense costs, their welfare budgets would have faced even greater financial pressure. Finland's fiscal difficulties might well have emerged sooner.

Now imagine attempting to replicate this economic model in the United States, a country with more than 340 million people, enormous existing entitlement obligations, substantial national debt and global military responsibilities. Expanding government spending on such a scale would require difficult choices involving higher taxation, additional borrowing or reductions in other areas of public spending. The American middle class would not be immune from those costs.

Europe's welfare programs are often advertised to Americans as benefits without mentioning the sacrifices required to sustain them. Higher taxes, weaker incentives for investment, reduced disposable income and slower economic growth are all potential consequences of excessive government expansion.

America should be addressing the underlying reasons why healthcare, housing and higher education have become so expensive. Increasing competition, reducing unnecessary bureaucracy, encouraging innovation and expanding supply are better long-term objectives than simply transferring more of the bill to taxpayers.

The objective of economic policy should be to make ordinary citizens wealthier and more financially independent, not to make them increasingly dependent on government programs. A country cannot tax and redistribute its way to unlimited prosperity.

America should learn from Europe's economic difficulties rather than assume that importing its welfare model will solve America's problems. Sustainable prosperity requires productivity, investment, entrepreneurship, fiscal responsibility and economic freedom. Government promises cannot substitute for the wealth necessary to finance them.
